profile.name: Dhathathreyan Natarajan
profile.headline: Data Science & Economics at NUS
profile.about:
I'm a Data Science and Economics undergraduate at the National University of Singapore, and at heart I'm a deeply curious person. My first instinct with anything new is to ask why: why a model behaves the way it does, why a market moves, why a result doesn't match my expectations. Knowing that something works is never quite enough for me. I want to understand how and why it works, so I go into each topic in depth until the logic makes sense from first principles. That habit has served me well in data science and economics, where the most valuable insights usually sit beneath the surface.

People who work with me would describe me as a jovial team player. I enjoy the energy of working with others, I like keeping spirits up when the pressure is on, and I'm at my best when the whole team is pulling in the same direction. At the same time, I hold myself to a high standard on the details: the assumption buried in a spreadsheet, the mislabelled chart, the line of code that quietly leaks data. My time as a Combat Engineer Officer in the Singapore Armed Forces, where small oversights carry real consequences, reinforced that discipline, and I bring it to every project and team I'm part of.

Outside of work and study, I like to stay active and keep exploring. I enjoy sports and love going on adventures, whether that means travelling somewhere unfamiliar, trying something I've never done before or seeing a familiar place from a new angle. Travelling has taught me to adapt quickly, stay comfortable with the unknown and connect with people from very different backgrounds. Those are the same qualities I bring to new problems, new teams and new challenges.

items.name: Python
items.note: A popular, readable programming language, used across these projects for data analysis, machine learning and automation.

items.name: Pandas
items.note: A Python library for working with tables of data, like Excel but in code, so every analysis is repeatable.

items.name: NumPy
items.note: Fast maths on large sets of numbers. Most Python data tools are built on top of it.

items.name: scikit-learn
items.note: A Python toolkit of ready-made machine learning models, plus tools to test them fairly.

items.name: R
items.note: A programming language built for statistics, used for the regression and predictive modelling projects.

items.name: Flask
items.note: A lightweight Python framework for building web apps and APIs. It powers this website's admin page and the ARROW briefing API.

items.name: Data structures & algorithms
items.note: Ways of organising data (lists, trees, graphs, hash tables) and step-by-step methods that make programs fast.

items.name: HTML, CSS & JavaScript
items.note: The languages of the web: structure, styling and interactivity. This website is built with them.

items.name: Random Forest
items.note: Many decision trees vote together on the answer. Robust, and a strong baseline for predictions.

items.name: XGBoost
items.note: Builds trees one after another, each fixing the previous one's mistakes. Often the most accurate model on table-style data.

items.name: LSTM (Keras)
items.note: A neural network with memory, designed for sequences such as hourly weather or daily prices.

items.name: Hybrid LSTM-XGBoost
items.note: An LSTM learns patterns over time, then hands those patterns to XGBoost to make the final prediction.

items.name: Bayesian optimisation (Optuna)
items.note: A smart way to tune a model's settings: it learns from earlier trials which settings to try next, instead of guessing.

items.name: k-NN
items.note: Predicts from the most similar past examples, e.g. a flat's price from the prices of the most similar flats.

items.name: Decision trees
items.note: A flowchart of yes/no questions that ends in a prediction. Easy to explain to anyone.

items.name: PCA / PCR
items.note: Squeezes many overlapping variables into a few combined ones that keep most of the information, then runs a regression on them.

items.name: Cross-validation
items.note: Testing a model on several slices of data it hasn't seen, for an honest estimate of how well it will really perform.

items.name: Linear regression
items.note: Measures how an outcome moves with its drivers, e.g. how much each extra square metre adds to a flat's price.

items.name: Box-Cox transformation
items.note: A test for the best way to reshape skewed data (for example, taking logs) so a model's assumptions hold.

items.name: Residual diagnostics
items.note: Checking a model's errors for patterns. A good model leaves errors that look like random noise.

items.name: Stepwise selection (AIC)
items.note: Adding or removing variables one at a time, keeping a change only if the model explains more without becoming needlessly complex.

items.name: Multicollinearity (VIF)
items.note: Detects when input variables overlap so much that the model can't tell their separate effects apart.

items.name: Stationarity testing (ADF, KPSS)
items.note: Checks whether a time series behaves consistently over time, which many forecasting methods rely on.

items.name: ACF / PACF
items.note: Charts of how strongly a value relates to its own past values. They reveal cycles, like a daily pattern in humidity.

items.name: Probability & mathematical statistics
items.note: The theory of uncertainty and estimation: distributions, maximum likelihood, confidence intervals and hypothesis tests.

items.name: RAG pipelines
items.note: Retrieval-augmented generation: the AI first looks up relevant documents, then answers using only them, so answers are grounded and checkable.

items.name: LangChain
items.note: A Python framework for connecting language models to documents, prompts and other tools.

items.name: ChromaDB
items.note: A database that stores text as numbers (embeddings) so you can search by meaning rather than exact words.

items.name: Hugging Face
items.note: A platform hosting thousands of open-source AI models that can be used directly from code.

items.name: Sentence embeddings
items.note: Turning sentences into lists of numbers so that texts with similar meanings sit close together.

items.name: Prompt design

projects.title: ARROW: Maritime Intelligence Platform
projects.summary: A shipbroking platform that pairs an AI market briefing (RAG) with route optimisation and fuel-strategy analysis.
projects.description:
Shipbrokers negotiate fixtures between shipowners and charterers using regulations, market reports and route knowledge scattered across dozens of documents. For the ARROW case competition our team built a web platform that brings this together: define a cargo and route, plan the voyage, compare fuel strategies, and get an AI-written market briefing grounded in real regulatory and market documents.

My part was the RAG pipeline behind the briefings and the AI assistant, which answers questions using only information drawn from the document library.

mindmap.label: Problem
items: Brokers juggle regulations, reports and routes

approach: Indexed a library of 15 maritime documents (SOLAS, MARPOL, the ISM and ISPS codes, BIMCO charter parties, ISO 8217 fuel standards and Veson market reports) into a Chroma vector store using all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence embeddings.
Retrieved the most relevant passages for each voyage's inputs (ports, cargo, fuel type and laycan dates) and listed the source documents alongside each answer.

Prompted Mistral-7B-Instruct (via Hugging Face) to write a structured 800–900-word broker briefing covering route risks, cargo market conditions, fuel and compliance costs, negotiation leverage and valuation ranges, using only the retrieved context.
Served the pipeline as a Flask API, packaged with Docker, that feeds the platform's dashboard and chat assistant.

The team's route optimiser generated 3,789 candidate sea routes between export and import ports (direct and via hub ports), flagged high-risk war zones and ranked routes by distance, port charges and expected demurrage.
The fuel-strategy module compares a baseline fuel mix with alternative fuels and energy-saving devices over a vessel's life, including carbon pooling prices, discounting, ROI and price sensitivity.
highlights: End-to-end prototype: web dashboard, RAG briefing API and route optimiser working together
Every briefing lists the regulatory and market documents it draws from, so brokers can check each claim
3,789 pre-computed routes, mapped interactively with Folium

tables.title: RAG pipeline configuration
rows: Small and fast, good semantic search quality
Search by meaning; stays on disk between runs
Open-source, runs through the Hugging Face API
Keeps answers factual rather than creative

tables.title: Platform modules
rows: Writes a negotiation briefing for a route and cargo
Ranks routes by distance, port costs and war-zone risk
Compares fuel and retrofit scenarios with ROI and DCF
Shows Baltic indices, fuel prices and charter rates

projects.conclusion: The prototype showed that a small open-source model can produce useful, trustworthy briefings when retrieval does the heavy lifting. Because Mistral-7B was restricted to the retrieved passages and every answer lists its sources, each claim in a briefing can be traced back to the regulation or market report it came from. Together with route ranking and fuel-strategy analysis, the platform covers the main questions a broker asks before negotiating a fixture.
projects.learnings: This was my first time building a RAG system end to end. I learnt that answer quality depends far more on what you retrieve than on the model itself: how documents are split into chunks, which inputs you search with, and how strictly the prompt keeps the model within its context. I also picked up practical engineering habits, like keeping API keys out of the code, packaging a service in Docker so teammates can run it, and designing an API that a front end built by someone else can call. Working on one part of a larger team system taught me to agree on interfaces early.

projects.title: Nanyang Capital Stock Pitch: Capcom vs Corteva
projects.summary: We built full buy cases for two very different stocks, Capcom and Corteva, then chose to pitch Corteva (BUY, US$66.33 target).
projects.description:
A stock pitch only gets one pick, so we analysed two candidates in full before committing: Capcom (TSE: 9697), the Japanese games publisher behind Resident Evil and Monster Hunter, and Corteva (NYSE: CTVA), the US seed and crop protection company spun out of DowDuPont.

Each got the full treatment: a revenue model built from business segments, a discounted cash flow (DCF) valuation, a peer comparison and a risk review. With both cases side by side, we decided to pitch Corteva.

mindmap.label: Capcom case
items: Variant view on the Monster Hunter Wilds sell-off

approach: Capcom: compiled five years of financials and projected revenue by segment (Digital Contents, Arcade Operations, Amusement Equipment, Other) to FY2028, driven by unit sales of major titles and catalog growth.

Capcom: valued the company with a DCF (WACC 8.7%, terminal growth 2.5%) weighted with peer multiples and probability-weighted bear, base and bull scenarios, and wrote a variant view on five market concerns.
Corteva: split revenue into seed and crop protection, forecast each by region from price, volume and currency effects, and modelled restructuring savings and their effect on margins.
Corteva: built a DCF (CAPM cost of equity, 2.5% terminal growth) with a WACC and terminal-growth sensitivity table, then cross-checked it against a football field of peer multiples.
Assessed each company's competitive position (moat, Porter's five forces) and key risks, then compared the two cases on upside, downside and conviction.
highlights: Final pick: Corteva, BUY with a US$66.33 target (+25.7%)
Corteva's downside valuation (US$56.10) still sat above its share price
Capcom case: BUY with a ¥4,800 base target (+30.8%), but a bear case of −24%

tables.title: The two cases side by side
rows: DCF, cross-checked with a comps football field

tables.title: Corteva vs agricultural peers
tables.note: Multiples as of August 2024. BASF is excluded because its P/E was not meaningful at the time.

charts.title: Corteva: where the US$66.33 target sits (implied share price, US$)
charts.note: Comparable-company bars show the 25th–75th percentile of implied share prices; the DCF bar runs from the downside case to the base case.

projects.conclusion: Both companies came out as BUYs. Capcom offered more upside in the base case (+30.8%) but a wider spread of outcomes: its bear case implied a 24% loss if game launches disappointed. Corteva's base case offered +25.7%, its target sat slightly above the median of the peer-multiple ranges, and even its downside valuation of US$56.10 was above the share price at the time. After weighing both, we pitched Corteva.
projects.learnings: Running two full analyses side by side taught me that a stock pitch is as much about the downside as the upside. I learnt to build revenue from business-segment drivers instead of extrapolating totals, to cross-check a DCF against market multiples (a football field makes it obvious when a target is out of line), and how sensitive a DCF is to WACC and terminal growth. Writing the variant view for Capcom forced me to state exactly where we disagreed with the market and what would prove us right.

projects.title: Weather Humidity Forecasting
projects.summary: Forecasting relative humidity 1, 6 and 24 hours ahead with Random Forest, XGBoost, LSTM and a hybrid LSTM-XGBoost model.
projects.role: Built the forecasting models; wrote the Pandas preprocessing pipeline and the stationarity and correlation analysis
projects.description: Relative humidity matters for weather forecasting, public health and environmental monitoring, but it's hard to predict because weather variables interact in complex, non-linear ways. Using 100,057 hourly observations from 2010 to 2021, we built and compared four machine learning models to forecast humidity 1, 6 and 24 hours ahead, without using current humidity as an input.
approach: Explored the data first: correlation matrix, ACF and PACF plots, ADF and KPSS stationarity tests and rolling statistics, which revealed a strong 24-hour cycle.
Wrote the preprocessing pipeline in Pandas: removed physically impossible readings, standardised features and built 1, 6 and 24-hour lag windows without leaking the target.
Built a Random Forest baseline, then XGBoost with seasonal, lag, difference and interaction features, validated with time-series cross-validation.
Built LSTM models in Keras and tuned units, dropout, learning rate, batch size and epochs separately for each horizon using Bayesian optimisation (Optuna).
Built a hybrid model that feeds patterns learned by the LSTM into a tuned XGBoost model.
highlights: XGBoost was the best model at every horizon: MAE 0.046 (1h), 0.064 (6h) and 0.080 (24h)
Errors comparable to the 5–10% typical of human forecasters
The hybrid LSTM-XGBoost didn't beat its parts, and we explained why

tables.title: Mean absolute error by model and forecast horizon (lower is better)
tables.note: Relative humidity runs from 0 to 1, so an MAE of 0.046 means predictions were off by about 4.6 percentage points on average.

charts.title: Forecast error by horizon (MAE, lower is better)

projects.conclusion: XGBoost delivered the lowest error at every horizon. Its tree structure makes the most of engineered lag, difference and interaction features, and its built-in regularisation copes well with noisy weather data. The LSTM matched it at one hour but drifted further out, and the hybrid didn't outperform either model on its own, probably because the extra layer added complexity without new information. All models got worse as the horizon grew, as expected. The biggest limitation was that current humidity wasn't allowed as an input; real forecasting would add it, along with radar or satellite data.
projects.learnings: Time-series data punishes shortcuts. I learnt to check stationarity and seasonality before modelling, to split data in time order, and to build lag features without leaking the answer into the inputs. I saw that a well-engineered gradient-boosting model can beat a deep network on tabular data, and that a more complex model (our hybrid) has to earn its place on the test set. I also learnt to tune hyperparameters with Bayesian optimisation instead of guesswork. Splitting the work across four people taught me the value of a reproducible notebook with clear run instructions.

projects.title: HDB Resale Price Regression Model
projects.summary: A statistically rigorous linear model of Singapore HDB resale prices that explains 88.6% of price variation.
projects.description: The goal was to build the best linear regression model for HDB resale prices that also satisfies the standard regression assumptions, so its coefficients can be trusted and interpreted. The data covers 2,456 resale transactions from July 2020 (data.gov.sg).
approach: Explored the price distribution (right-skewed, skewness 1.04) and engineered features: remaining lease in decimal years, storey midpoints and flat age.
Found perfect multicollinearity between remaining lease, flat age and lease start date (|r| = 0.9993) and kept only one of them.
Fitted a baseline model, then used Box-Cox analysis (optimal λ = −0.38) to compare log and reciprocal square-root transformations, choosing the log for interpretability.
Ran stepwise AIC selection, VIF checks, influence diagnostics (Cook's distance) and full residual checks for normality, constant variance, linearity and independence.
Interpreted every coefficient as a percentage price effect.
highlights: Adjusted R² of 0.886, up from 0.841 for the untransformed baseline
All key regression assumptions checked; no highly influential points (max Cook's D = 0.089)

tables.title: Comparing the candidate models
tables.note: The Box-Cox model fit marginally better, but its coefficients can't be read as price effects, so I chose the log model.

tables.title: What drives the price (final model)
rows: Central Area vs Ang Mo Kio
tables.note: Each effect holds the other factors constant.

charts.title: Town premium or discount vs Ang Mo Kio (%)

projects.conclusion: The final log-linear model explains 88.6% of the variation in resale prices and predicts within 8.62% on average. It satisfies the key assumptions: residuals are approximately normal with constant variance, relationships are linear, and multicollinearity is under control. The only caveat is mild autocorrelation (Durbin-Watson 1.28), which is expected because nearby towns move together. The results match Singapore's familiar price gradient: central and southern towns command large premiums while northern and western towns are more affordable.
projects.learnings: This project taught me that a good regression model is one you can defend, not just the one with the highest R². Box-Cox pointed to a transformation that fit slightly better, but I chose the log because its coefficients translate directly into percentage price effects people can use. I learnt the full adequacy-checking routine (residual plots, normality and independence tests, VIF and Cook's distance) and how to justify decisions such as dropping perfectly collinear variables. Compared with my first-year HDB project, it showed me the difference between predicting well and explaining why.

figures.label: Predicted vs actual resale prices: points close to the line mean accurate predictions

projects.title: Predicting HDB Resale Prices with Machine Learning
projects.summary: Comparing linear regression, decision trees, k-NN and principal component regression to predict HDB resale prices.
projects.description: Buyers and sellers make better decisions when they understand what drives HDB resale prices. Working with a dataset of flat characteristics, I reduced 230 candidate predictors to 133, then built and compared four predictive models, judging them by RMSE and by margin of error against the mean price of about $497,000.

mindmap.label: Evaluate
items: Margin of error vs mean price

approach: Log-transformed the right-skewed resale price to stabilise variance and reduce the pull of extreme values.
Used a 4,000 / 2,000 train-test split and 10-fold cross-validation for every model.
Built a linear model with forward selection (91 predictors), a decision tree tuned on its complexity parameter, and k-NN tuned on k.
Applied PCA to keep 95% of the variance, cutting 133 predictors to 69 components, then fitted a principal component regression.
highlights: Principal component regression was the most accurate: RMSE $40,092, an 8.06% margin of error
Beat linear regression (10.34%), the decision tree (11.07%) and k-NN (15.12%)

tables.title: Model comparison on the test set
tables.note: Margin of error = RMSE ÷ mean resale price ($497,486).

charts.title: Prediction error by model (RMSE, lower is better)

projects.conclusion: Principal component regression was the clear winner: by compressing 133 overlapping predictors into 69 components, it removed noise and produced the tightest predictions, with most points close to the perfect-prediction line. Linear regression and the decision tree performed similarly (10–11% error), while k-NN struggled with so many features. The remaining error suggests that economic factors outside the dataset matter too, such as housing grants like the 2019 Enhanced CPF Housing Grant.
projects.learnings: This was my first full machine learning project. I learnt the core workflow: split the data first, validate with cross-validation, tune each model's key setting and compare on a held-out test set using a metric people understand (RMSE in dollars). Cutting 133 predictors to 69 components showed me how much redundancy real data carries, and k-NN's weak result showed how some methods break down with many features. I also made, and caught, a classic mistake: accidentally leaving the price inside the training features. Now I check for data leakage every time.

figures.label: Actual vs predicted prices for all four models (red line = perfect prediction)

projects.title: Raising Singapore's Female Labour Force Participation
projects.summary: NTU x MOM essay competition: a data-driven country similarity index and a policy proposal for Singapore.
projects.role: Built the machine learning similarity index; co-wrote the policy analysis
projects.description:
Singapore's female labour force participation rate (FLFPR) was 61.25% in 2024, behind global leaders like Iceland at 70.3%. Policies only transfer well between similar countries, so before studying what other countries do, we used data to find the countries most like Singapore.

We then evaluated their parental leave, childcare, equal pay and four-day week policies through three economic frameworks, and designed a proposal suited to Singapore.

mindmap.label: Question
items: How can Singapore raise its FLFPR?

mindmap.label: Data
items: Cost of living and purchasing power

approach: Combined country-level data on female participation trends, female working hours, GDP per capita, purchasing power, cost of living and a broader similarity index.
Cleaned and matched country names across sources with fuzzy matching, and filled missing values using the most similar countries.
Weighted each metric by its correlation with female participation and scored every country's distance from Singapore, which identified Iceland, New Zealand and Vietnam as the closest comparators.
Evaluated their policies through Human Capital Theory, Feminist Economics and Institutional Path Dependence.
Proposed Community-Supported Workplace Childcare Co-operatives: employer-supported, government-subsidised childcare hubs with AI-driven scheduling and a 32-hour work week.
highlights: Comparator countries chosen with data rather than intuition
A concrete, Singapore-specific proposal grounded in evidence from Iceland, New Zealand, Vietnam and Quebec

tables.title: What we learnt from each comparator
rows: Gender-neutral parental leave, subsidised childcare, 4-day week trials (2015–2019)
Flexible work kept productivity while raising men's share of caregiving
Flexible leave, free early childhood education, Unilever 4-day week trial (2022)
Cheaper childcare and flexibility keep mothers attached to work
Firms themselves can make childcare accessible
Associated with a 7.7% rise in FLFPR

projects.conclusion: Our comparison found a common thread: countries with higher female participation reduce the 'motherhood penalty' by making childcare affordable and work flexible. We combined Iceland's flexibility with Vietnam's employer-led model into a proposal for Singapore, Community-Supported Workplace Childcare Co-operatives, which fits the Smart Nation vision and Singapore's collectivist culture. Quebec's 7.7% rise in FLFPR after introducing universal childcare suggests the potential impact.
projects.learnings: I learnt that 'which countries should we learn from?' can be answered with data rather than intuition. Building the similarity index taught me practical data wrangling: matching country names across sources, filling gaps sensibly and choosing weights that reflect what matters for the question. Writing with Clarence taught me to turn quantitative findings into an argument policymakers can follow, grounded in economic theory.

projects.summary: A Python system that pulls live and historical equity data and generates rule-based trading signals.
projects.description: An ongoing personal project to build a disciplined, testable trading system instead of trading on gut feel.
approach: Pull live and historical equity data through broker and market-data APIs.
Generate rule-based signals from indicators such as moving averages and RSI.
Design parameter-sensitivity and out-of-sample tests before backtesting, to avoid overfitting to past data.
projects.conclusion: Still in progress. Results will be added once out-of-sample testing is complete.
projects.learnings: Even before backtesting, I've learnt why so many strategies fail on new data: it's easy to tune parameters until the past looks great. Designing the sensitivity and out-of-sample tests first keeps me honest about whether a signal is real.
